slides.say: x and y are integers. Given: three is smaller than x plus y, in absolute value. Which of the following is possible but not necessarily true?
Unlike the last few questions, this is a technique question. And before we start, let's understand the wording. Possible, but not necessarily true.

So anything that's never true is not possible, and it's out. And anything that's always true is necessarily true, so it's out too. We want the one that's sometimes true and sometimes not. [short pause] Two ways, the rules first, and then plugging in numbers.

[short pause] Our first method. Number one looks like the given, with brackets instead of bars, and a square. Both sides of the given are positive, so I'm allowed to square them. Three squared is nine.
And x plus y in absolute value, squared, is the same as x plus y, squared. A square doesn't care about the sign. So number one is always true, and it's out.
And there's a much simpler way to see it. Bars and an even power behave the same way. What's true with bars is true with a square.
Number two, let's leave it for the end.

Number three. The absolute value of x y, against the absolute value of x times the absolute value of y. Remember, you can split the bars over multiplication. So these two are always equal, never smaller. Never true, so it's out.
Number four. Inside the bars I have five x plus five y. Take out the common factor five, and split the bars. That's five times the absolute value of x plus y.

So it says something is smaller than five times itself. That's true for every positive number. Could it fail? Only if x plus y were zero, but the given says it's more than three in absolute value. So it's always true, out.

Three are out, so in the exam you'd circle number two. Here, let's see why it's right. The rule from the lesson says the absolute value of a sum is smaller than or equal to the sum of the absolute values. They're equal when x and y have the same sign, and it's smaller when the signs are opposite. So sometimes true, sometimes not. Number two is our answer.

[pause] Our second method, plugging in numbers. I'll try one pair with the same sign and one with opposite signs, because signs are what the bars care about. First, x four and y one, small and easy. Four plus one is five, and five is bigger than three, so they fit the given.
Number one, twenty-five is bigger than nine, true. Number two, five smaller than five? No. Number three, four smaller than four? No. Number four, five smaller than twenty-five, true.

Now opposite signs. Why x six and y negative two? Because with opposite signs they cancel, so I need one of them much bigger, to keep the sum above three. Six minus two is four, and four is bigger than three, so they fit.

Number one, sixteen bigger than nine, true. Number two, four smaller than six plus two, that's eight. True this time. Number three, twelve smaller than twelve? No again. Number four, four smaller than twenty, true.
So number two was false once and true once. That's exactly possible but not necessarily. Number three was never true, and numbers one and four were true both times. Number two.
Which way is better? If you know the rules, you can mark this one in seconds. If not, two pairs, same sign and opposite signs, will get you there. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
